$comment: Everyday stories, noun Concept, part 3 of 4 (field.*, fieldConvention.defaults, index, invariant, lifecycle, lifecycleState, lifecycleTransition). Same style rules as stories-pilot.json. Owner reviews each part.

stories.field.access: In a clinic the receptionist may see a patient's name but not the diagnosis, while the doctor sees both. Field access works one box at a time: who may read it and who may change it, per record. A box you may not read is simply left out of the answer, and a change you may not make is refused whole.
stories.field.connectable: Staff know a product by its code 'P-100', not by a long hidden id. Marking a unique code box as an anchor lets other concepts point at it. An order line can then refer to 'P-100' directly, and stays within the same company's data.
stories.field.default: A new ticket should start with priority 'Normal' unless someone says otherwise. Default is a fixed value stored when the person leaves the box empty on creation. If they type something, theirs wins.
stories.field.description: A box called 'Ref' means nothing to a newcomer. Description is one sentence saying what the box holds, such as 'The supplier's own invoice number'. It appears as help in the screen and is read by AI assistants that write the app.
stories.field.domainType: Ten different boxes hold a postal code and each needs the same five-digit rule. Domain type says 'this box is a PostalCode'. It then inherits the stored kind, the checks, the tidying and the look from that one definition.
stories.field.duplicationPolicy: A list of tags on an article should not have 'sale' twice. Duplication policy decides whether elements that share the same identity are allowed or refused in a list box. One word turns on the guard.
stories.field.file: A claim form needs a photo of the damaged car. A file box accepts uploads, and you decide which kinds, how big, and whether one or many. What is stored is a small receipt for the file, never the bytes in the record itself.
stories.field.id: Every record needs a number on its tag so it cannot be mistaken for another. The id box is that tag, the record's identifier. By habit it is a long unique code and is called 'id'. The app creates it, and people never type it.
stories.field.itemIdentityField: In a list of order items, two items are 'the same' when they have the same product code. Item identity field names that box. Together with the duplication policy, it tells the app when two list elements are really one.
stories.field.items: A box that holds a list needs to say what each element looks like, such as 'a short text up to 20 letters'. Items is that description, applied to every element of the list.
stories.field.max: Nobody can sell minus five or 500 discount percent. Max sets the largest number a box accepts, inclusive. Above it, the form says so while the person is still typing.
stories.field.maxItems: A product page may show at most five photos. Max items sets how many elements a list box may hold. The sixth is refused with a clear message.
stories.field.min: A discount cannot be below zero and a seat count cannot be zero. Min sets the smallest number a box accepts, inclusive. Anything lower is refused while the person types.
stories.field.minItems: An invoice with no lines is just a piece of paper. Min items sets how many elements a list box needs at least. The record cannot be saved with fewer.
stories.field.minLength: A password of one letter is no password. Min length sets the fewest characters a text box accepts. The app tells the person how many more they need before saving.
stories.field.name: Each box on a card has a title, such as 'phone'. The field's name is that title, and it is also the column in the database and the key in the app's web interface. It cannot be repeated inside the same concept.
stories.field.picker: A box that points at a customer opens a small search window, and sometimes you want it to allow several choices or only active customers. Picker sets those two things for that window: a filter and whether more than one may be chosen.
stories.field.precision: An amount like 12345.67 has seven digits in total. Precision says how many digits a decimal number may have altogether, up to 38. It stops a typo like an extra zero from turning into a million.
stories.field.properties: An address is not one piece of text but several: street, number, city. A structured box holds them together, and Properties lists its named parts, each with its own description and checks. On the form it behaves like a single box, but the data stays tidy.
stories.field.renamedFrom: You rename the box 'tel' to 'phone', and the old column still has all the numbers. Renamed from tells NPDev it is the same box under a new name, so the column is renamed and the data is kept.
stories.field.scale: Prices have two digits after the point, exchange rates have six. Scale says how many digits a decimal number keeps after the point. Extra digits are not silently invented or lost in a report.
stories.field.type: A box for a birth date, one for a price and one for a yes-or-no each hold a different kind of thing. Type says which kind: text, whole number, decimal, date, true or false, a choice from a list, a link to another record, a file or a structure. Everything else follows from it.
stories.field.ui: A box holds the same data whatever it looks like, but people want a label, a hint, a nicer control or a group. This keyword gathers all those looks for one box. The data stays the same, only the way it is shown changes.
stories.field.uid: A box is renamed and its name no longer matches the database column. A uid is a fingerprint stamped on the box once and never reused. When the fingerprint matches, NPDev knows it is the same box, and the data is kept without any extra hint.
stories.field.uniqueItems: The tags on an article should all be different. Unique items says that no two elements of a list box may be equal. One setting stops the same tag from being added twice.
stories.fieldConvention.defaults: A rule such as 'names ending in Dt are dates' needs to say what such a box becomes: its kind, and perhaps its size. Defaults are those settings, always a type and optionally lengths or limits. A box that states its own type is never touched.
stories.index.fields: An address book is faster when sorted by surname, then first name. Index fields name the boxes an index covers, in order. The database can jump straight to the right page for searches on those boxes.
stories.index.name: Every index has a label in the database, which helps when someone has to look inside. Name is that label. If you leave it out, NPDev makes one from the concept and the boxes.
stories.index.unique: A shop may have only one price list per product and day. A unique index forbids two records with the same combination of values in the indexed boxes. The database itself refuses the repeat, whatever screen tried it.
stories.invariant.expr: A shorter spelling of 'expression', for people who prefer it. The one-line condition has to be true for a record to be saved. The result is exactly the same.
stories.invariant.fields: No two guests may book the same room on the same night. For a uniqueness rule, fields lists the boxes whose values must be unique together. Either one may repeat, but the pair cannot.
stories.invariant.name: When a record breaks a rule, the message must say which one: 'room-double-booking'. Name is the rule's label, shown in the error and used when another concept wants to replace this rule.
stories.invariant.override: A VIP concept inherits a rule 'discount up to 10%' but allows more. Override says 'my rule with this name replaces the inherited one'. The specialised concept keeps all the other rules unchanged.
stories.invariant.specializes: A refined rule says 'I am the stricter version of that inherited one'. Specializes names the inherited rule it builds upon, so people reading the model can follow where the rule came from.
stories.invariant.type: There are two kinds of rule: 'these boxes must be unique together' and 'this condition must be true'. Type picks which one. That decides whether you then list fields or write an expression.
stories.lifecycle.states: A parcel is packed, shipped or delivered, and each stage deserves a name, a label and a mark for first and last. States lists them. If you leave it out, NPDev reads the stages from the moves you allow.
stories.lifecycle.statusField: The current stage of a parcel has to be stored somewhere. Status field names the choice box that holds it. If you do not say, NPDev uses a box called 'status'.
stories.lifecycle.transitions: Packed may go to shipped, shipped to delivered, and nothing else. Transitions list those allowed moves, at least one. Any move you do not list is refused, however the request arrives.
stories.lifecycleState.allowedActions: A parcel that is packed can be shipped or cancelled, but not rated. Allowed actions lists the buttons offered while a record is in this stage. In other stages, those buttons are simply not there.
stories.lifecycleState.initial: Every new parcel starts as 'packed'. Initial marks the stage a new record is born in. People never have to choose it.
stories.lifecycleState.label: The stored word may be 'IN_TRANSIT', but the screen should say 'On its way'. Label is the text people see for a stage, so the screen speaks their language.
stories.lifecycleState.metadata: Sometimes the author wants to leave a note on a stage, such as 'billing starts here'. Metadata is a small free notebook for plain notes. The app carries it along and does not act on it.
stories.lifecycleState.terminal: A delivered parcel stays delivered. Terminal marks a final stage: no move may leave it, the record becomes read-only and the board shows the column as finished. The validator refuses any rule that tries to leave it.
stories.lifecycleState.value: A stage needs a steady name that the database stores, even if the screen text changes: 'DELIVERED'. Value is that stored word, one of the choices of the status box.
stories.lifecycleTransition.action: A move such as 'Cancel order' needs a confirmation, a success message and a warning colour. This keyword gathers how the move's button is presented, so the person understands what is about to happen.
stories.lifecycleTransition.actionLabel: The move from packed to shipped may appear to people as a button 'Send it off'. Action label is the caption of that button, in plain words and in each language.
stories.lifecycleTransition.event: When a parcel is shipped, the customer should get a message. This keyword names the event announced with that move, so other parts of the app can react as it happens, without anyone calling them by hand.
stories.lifecycleTransition.from: A move starts somewhere. From is the stage the record is in before it, such as 'packed'. Only records in that stage can take this move.
stories.lifecycleTransition.guard: A parcel may ship only if it has an address. The guard is a condition on the record that must be true before this move is allowed. While it is false, the button is not offered or the move is refused.
stories.lifecycleTransition.metadata: A note on a move, such as 'agreed with legal', for those who read the model. Metadata is a free notebook that the app carries along and does not act on.
stories.lifecycleTransition.requiredPayload: Cancelling a ride needs a reason; shipping needs a carrier. Required payload lists the boxes of the record that must hold a value before the move can happen. If one is empty, the person is asked to fill it.
stories.lifecycleTransition.to: A move ends somewhere. To is the stage the record is in after it, such as 'shipped'. Together with 'from', it describes one allowed step.
